proposed_integration_patches.replacement_text:
The dome’s stated observable does not exist in its own source. The dome claims a ‘−6.5 μGal gravity anomaly at eclipse maximum’ and cites Wang et al. (2000, Phys. Rev. D 62, 041101), a LaCoste-Romberg spring-gravimeter record from Mohe during the 9 March 1997 total eclipse. But the signal in that dataset is two near-symmetric ‘gravity anomaly valleys’ of about 6–7 μGal at first and last contact — the edges of the eclipse — not at maximum. The same team’s reanalysis of the same dataset, Yang & Wang (2002, Astrophys. Space Sci. 282, 245–253), states it plainly: ‘no significant anomaly during the very solar eclipse was found’, while reaffirming the two contact-phase valleys as ‘the anomaly phenomenon observed and reported for the first time in the literature.’ The valleys are real and were reaffirmed, not withdrawn — but they sit at the wrong phase for the dome. At eclipse maximum, exactly where the dome locates its −6.5 μGal, the source reports null.

Why ‘the effect is intermittent’ cannot rescue it. A dome defender will object that Allais-type eclipse anomalies are reported as intermittent and eclipse-geometry-dependent, so a null at one eclipse cannot refute a positive at another. Granted — but that defense protects the phenomenon, not the dome’s use of it. The dome’s problem is internal to the single dataset it cites: at the phase the dome names (maximum), the source reports no signal, and the signal that does exist (the contact-phase valleys) is at a phase the dome does not claim. Intermittency can explain why different eclipses differ; it cannot move a signal from first/last contact to eclipse maximum inside one dataset. The valleys themselves also come with a conventional explanation from the source’s own authors: the 2002 reanalysis attributes them to tilt effects from thermal stress and temperature change during the eclipse, and Van Flandern & Yang (2003, Phys. Rev. D 67, 022002) — co-authored by the same Xin-She Yang — develops the atmospheric account in detail (‘Allais gravity and pendulum effects during solar eclipses explained’). A contact-phase environmental artifact, explained by its own observers, demonstrates no electromagnetic-gravitational coupling. Finally, the dome states no rule for when an anomaly should occur or how large it should be, so a ‘hit’ is indistinguishable from selecting whichever reading happened to fluctuate. We are not adjudicating the Allais effect in general — only the dome’s adopted, phase-mislabeled, unpredicted number.

The coupling constant is a cross-event cherry-pick validated against itself. Domain #7 in monitor.py computes κ = 10.9 / 6.5 = 1.677 nT/μGal and compares it to a hardcoded KAPPA = 1.67 within a 5% tolerance — a 0.41% ‘agreement’ that is purely self-referential, because the ‘observed’ 1.677 is just the ratio of its own two hardcoded inputs; no gravimeter or magnetometer data is fetched. Worse, those two inputs are not co-measured: the −10.9 nT magnetic value is from the BOU 2017 eclipse (North America, INTERMAGNET) at eclipse maximum, while the −6.5 μGal gravity value is assigned to Mohe 1997 at eclipse maximum — the exact phase where the Mohe source reports null. The κ ratio does not just stitch together two different eclipses, continents, instruments, and decades; its gravity-side input does not exist at the claimed phase in its own source.

Corroboration from superior instruments. The dedicated superconducting-gravimeter test of the 11 August 1999 European eclipse, Mansinha, Ducarme, Hinderer, Meurers & van Ruymbeke (2001, J. Geod. Soc. Japan 47(1), 387–391), used four SG stations under or near the eclipse path (Uccle and Membach in Belgium, Strasbourg, Vienna) and found ‘no identifiable eclipse related change above the ambient noise’, bounding any gravitational shielding at γ < 10⁻¹⁶ m² kg⁻¹. We present this as supporting context, not as the decisive refutation: the load-bearing point is that the dome’s claimed observable is absent from its own source at the claimed phase and was never tied to a predictive rule, so the claim is unsubstantiated on its own terms — before any different-eclipse null is invoked.

The dome locates its −6.5 μGal anomaly at eclipse maximum — the one phase where its own sources (Wang et al. 2000; Yang & Wang 2002) report no significant signal. The contact-phase valleys that do exist were given a thermal/tilt explanation by the same authors (Yang & Wang 2002; Van Flandern & Yang 2003), and the dome offers no rule for when anomalies should occur. The 1.67 nT/μGal ‘coupling constant’ is a circular ratio of two hardcoded values from two different eclipses, validated against itself — and its gravity input is null at the claimed phase in the source.

Its own source papers report no significant signal at maximum — the only real dips occur at the start and end of the eclipse, and the source’s own authors explained those as heat-related instrument effects. The signal the dome cites does not exist at the phase it claims: its own source reports null at eclipse maximum. The dips that are real sit at the eclipse’s edges with a mundane thermal explanation, and the coupling constant is a circular ratio of numbers from two unrelated eclipses.
